messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jonathan is a 34-year-old Navy Officer who has been struggling with symptoms following a traumatic natural disaster that occurred during his deployment. The event was intense and overwhelming; he found himself trapped in a small space amidst the chaos of hurricane-force winds and flooding waters. The experience left him feeling utterly helpless and alone, despite being surrounded by fellow service members. Since then, Jonathan has found himself avoiding crowded places and any physical locations reminiscent of the disaster. Even the smell of alcohol—a memory associated with celebratory drinks before the storm—triggers a sense of unease that plunges him back into the trauma. These triggers have led him to isolate himself further from friends and family, as he believes seeing them will inevitably lead to another triggering moment. Jonathan's memories are vivid and visceral; when they come to mind, his body physically reenacts the position he was in during the event. He often finds himself reliving the experience with such clarity that it feels unreal, as if it could not have actually happened to him. This bodily reenactment exacerbates his sense of isolation, making him feel that he no longer belongs anywhere. Jonathan has come to believe that he deserves to suffer because of what happened and that there is a reason for his pain. These negative appraisals have reinforced the idea that he should avoid situations that remind him of the disaster, further isolating himself from friends and family. His maladaptive thinking has deepened his sense of loss; he used to be a happy person but now feels perpetually miserable. Jonathan's avoidance behaviors have concrete consequences in both his personal life and his work. He often skips social gatherings with colleagues and avoids bars or parties where the smell of alcohol might trigger memories. This behavior has led to strained relationships, as friends find it hard to understand why he is so distant and avoidant. At work, Jonathan’s performance has been affected by his inability to be in certain environments; he finds himself withdrawing from situations that require teamwork. His negative appraisals have also fueled a cycle of avoidance and maladaptive thinking. He feels isolated and set apart from others because these memories keep coming back with such force that it seems impossible for him to lead a normal life. The memory of being trapped in the hurricane has seeped into his daily routine, making him hyper-aware of potential triggers that could bring on another flood of emotions. Jonathan’s belief that he deserves to suffer makes him more likely to relive these memories and experience their vividness. He feels as if there is no escape from the trauma; it haunts him in every aspect of life. This cycle has tightened over time, making Jonathan feel increasingly trapped by his own thoughts and reactions. What finally brought Jonathan to seek help was a profound realization that he could not continue living this way. He was most afraid of losing himself completely to these memories and negative appraisals, but at the same time, he hoped for a chance to reclaim some sense of normalcy and happiness in his life.
